Pharmacodynamics: Atorvastatin Calcium Tablets, a synthetic lipid-lowering agent, is a selective, competitive inhibitor of 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase, the enzyme catalyzing the conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate, a rate-limiting step in cholesterol biosynthesis. By inhibiting this enzyme, Atorvastatin Calcium Tablets lower plasma cholesterol and lipoprotein levels by reducing cholesterol synthesis in the liver and increasing the number of hepatic Low Density Lipoprotein (LDL) receptors, enhancing LDL uptake and catabolism. This results in reduced LDL-Cholesterol (LDL-C) and LDL particles, as well as decreased Very Low Density Lipoprotein-Cholesterol (VLDL-C), serum triglycerides (TG), and Intermediate Density Lipoproteins (IDL), while increasing High Density Lipoprotein-Cholesterol (HDL-C). The lowering of total cholesterol, LDL-C, and ApoB has been shown to reduce the risk of cardiovascular events and mortality. Atorvastatin Calcium Tablets are effective in reducing LDL-C in patients with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia and have also been shown to improve endothelial dysfunction in patients with type II hyperlipidemia. The onset of action is rapid, with maximal plasma concentrations occurring within 1-2 hours, and the duration of action is sustained, with a bioavailability of 95-99% compared to an intravenous reference product. The pharmacodynamic effects of Atorvastatin Calcium Tablets are consistent across various patient populations, including those with mixed dyslipidemia, hypertriglyceridemia, and dysbetalipoproteinemia, and are not significantly affected by age or organ impairment.
Pregnancy Summary: JAMP Atorvastatin Tablets are contraindicated in pregnancy. The drug should be discontinued if pregnancy occurs during treatment. There is evidence from animal studies that atorvastatin may affect fetal development, with delayed development and reduced post-natal survival observed in rats. The risk to the fetus is unknown, but the drug should be used with caution in women of childbearing age who are highly unlikely to conceive.
Breastfeeding Summary: JAMP Atorvastatin Tablets are contraindicated in breastfeeding women. Atorvastatin is excreted in human milk, and its effects on the nursing infant are unknown. However, the drug's safety profile in pediatric patients suggests potential effects on the infant, including gastrointestinal and musculoskeletal issues. No information is available on the effects of atorvastatin on milk production/supply. Breastfeeding women should not take JAMP Atorvastatin Tablets.

Pharmacokinetics: Atorvastatin is rapidly absorbed after oral administration, with maximal plasma concentrations occurring within 1 to 2 hours, and its extent of absorption and plasma concentrations increase in proportion to the atorvastatin dose. The absolute bioavailability of atorvastatin is approximately 12%, and the systemic availability of HMG-CoA reductase inhibitory activity is approximately 30%, attributed to presystemic clearance in gastrointestinal mucosa and/or first-pass metabolism in the liver. Food decreases the rate and extent of drug absorption by approximately 25% and 9%, respectively, but LDL-C reduction and HDL-C elevation are similar when atorvastatin is given with and without food. Atorvastatin is extensively metabolized to ortho- and para-hydroxylated derivatives by cytochrome P-450 3A4 (CYP 3A4) and to various beta-oxidation products, with approximately 70% of circulating inhibitory activity for HMG-CoA reductase attributed to active metabolites. Atorvastatin is primarily eliminated in bile following hepatic and/or extrahepatic metabolism, with a mean plasma elimination half-life of approximately 14 hours, but the half-life for inhibitory activity for HMG-CoA reductase is 20 to 30 hours due to the contribution of longer-lived active metabolites. In special populations, plasma concentrations of atorvastatin are higher in healthy elderly subjects (approximately 40% for Cmax and 30% for AUC) compared with younger individuals, but LDL-C reduction is comparable to that seen in younger patient populations. Additionally, plasma concentrations of atorvastatin are similar in black and white subjects, but markedly increased (approximately 16-fold in Cmax and 11-fold in AUC) in patients with chronic alcoholic liver disease.

Pharmacodynamics: LIPITOR (atorvastatin calcium) is a synthetic lipid-lowering agent that exerts its pharmacodynamic effects through selective and competitive inhibition of 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme in cholesterol biosynthesis. By inhibiting this enzyme, LIPITOR reduces the conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate, thereby decreasing cholesterol synthesis in the liver and increasing the number of hepatic Low Density Lipoprotein (LDL) receptors, which enhances the uptake and catabolism of LDL. As a result, LIPITOR lowers plasma cholesterol and lipoprotein levels, including LDL-Cholesterol (LDL-C), Very Low Density Lipoprotein-Cholesterol (VLDL-C), serum triglycerides (TG), and Intermediate Density Lipoproteins (IDL), while increasing High Density Lipoprotein-Cholesterol (HDL-C). The reduction in LDL-C and the number of LDL particles, as well as the increase in HDL-C, are associated with a decreased risk of cardiovascular events and mortality. LIPITOR is effective in reducing LDL-C in patients with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, a condition that rarely responds to other lipid-lowering medications. In addition, LIPITOR has been shown to improve endothelial dysfunction in patients with type II hyperlipidemia, as evidenced by improved flow-mediated endothelium-dependent dilatation. The onset of action of LIPITOR is rapid, with maximal plasma concentrations occurring within 1-2 hours, and the duration of action is sustained, with LDL-C reduction and HDL-C elevation similar when administered with or without food. The pharmacodynamic effects of LIPITOR are not significantly affected by age, but may be influenced by organ impairment, such as liver or kidney disease, which can affect the drug's efficacy and safety.
Pregnancy Summary: LIPITOR (atorvastatin) is contraindicated in pregnancy. The drug has not been studied in pregnant women, and there is evidence from animal studies that it may affect fetal development. If pregnancy occurs during treatment, the drug should be discontinued. Fetal/neonatal risks include delayed development and reduced post-natal survival in rats.

Pharmacokinetics: Atorvastatin is rapidly absorbed after oral administration, with maximal plasma concentrations occurring within 1 to 2 hours, and its extent of absorption and plasma concentrations increase in proportion to the atorvastatin dose. The absolute bioavailability of atorvastatin is approximately 12%, and the systemic availability of HMG-CoA reductase inhibitory activity is approximately 30%, attributed to presystemic clearance in gastrointestinal mucosa and/or first-pass metabolism in the liver. Food decreases the rate and extent of drug absorption by approximately 25% and 9%, respectively, but LDL-C reduction and HDL-C elevation are similar when atorvastatin is given with and without food. Plasma atorvastatin concentrations are lower following evening administration compared to morning dosing, but LDL-C reduction and HDL-C elevation are the same regardless of the time of drug administration. Atorvastatin is extensively bound to plasma proteins, with a mean volume of distribution of approximately 381 liters, and is secreted in human milk. It is extensively metabolized to ortho- and para-hydroxylated derivatives by cytochrome P-450 3A4 (CYP 3A4) and to various beta-oxidation products, with approximately 70% of circulating inhibitory activity for HMG-CoA reductase attributed to active metabolites. Atorvastatin is eliminated primarily in bile following hepatic and/or extrahepatic metabolism, with a mean plasma elimination half-life of approximately 14 hours, but the half-life for inhibitory activity for HMG-CoA reductase is 20 to 30 hours due to the contribution of longer-lived active metabolites. Special population considerations include higher plasma concentrations in healthy elderly subjects, with comparable LDL-C reduction, and similar plasma concentrations in black and white subjects. However, plasma concentrations are markedly increased in patients with chronic alcoholic liver disease, and the lowest dose should be used in patients with moderate to severe renal insufficiency.

Pharmacodynamics: LIPITOR (atorvastatin calcium) is a synthetic lipid-lowering agent that selectively and competitively inhibits 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme in cholesterol biosynthesis. By inhibiting this enzyme, LIPITOR reduces the conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate, thereby lowering plasma cholesterol and lipoprotein levels. Additionally, LIPITOR increases the number of hepatic Low Density Lipoprotein (LDL) receptors on the cell surface, enhancing the uptake and catabolism of LDL. This results in reduced levels of LDL-Cholesterol (LDL-C) and the number of LDL particles, as well as decreased levels of Very Low Density Lipoprotein-Cholesterol (VLDL-C), serum triglycerides (TG), and Intermediate Density Lipoproteins (IDL). Conversely, LIPITOR increases High Density Lipoprotein-Cholesterol (HDL-C) levels. The pharmacodynamic effects of LIPITOR are evident in its ability to reduce the risk of cardiovascular events and mortality by lowering total cholesterol, LDL-C, and ApoB levels. LIPITOR has been shown to be effective in reducing LDL-C in patients with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, a condition that rarely responds to other lipid-lowering medications. Furthermore, LIPITOR has been demonstrated to improve endothelial dysfunction in patients with type II hyperlipidemia, as assessed by brachial ultrasound. The onset of action for LIPITOR is rapid, with maximal plasma concentrations occurring within 1-2 hours after oral administration. The duration of action is not explicitly stated, but the low systemic availability of atorvastatin (approximately 30%) suggests that the effects of LIPITOR may be sustained over an extended period. Special population considerations for PD effects include age, as the efficacy of LIPITOR has not been established in pediatric patients, and organ impairment, as the effects of LIPITOR may be altered in patients with hepatic or renal impairment.
Pregnancy Summary: LIPITOR (atorvastatin calcium) is contraindicated in pregnancy. There is no experience with LIPITOR in pregnant women, but animal studies suggest potential fetal toxicity. If pregnancy occurs during treatment, the drug should be discontinued. The most dangerous trimester is not specified, but fetal toxicity was observed in rats and rabbits at maternally toxic doses.

Pharmacokinetics: Atorvastatin is rapidly absorbed after oral administration, with maximal plasma concentrations occurring within 1 to 2 hours, and its extent of absorption and plasma concentrations increase in proportion to the atorvastatin dose. The absolute bioavailability of atorvastatin is approximately 12%, and the systemic availability of HMG-CoA reductase inhibitory activity is approximately 30%, attributed to pre-systemic clearance in gastrointestinal mucosa and/or first-pass metabolism in the liver. Food decreases the rate and extent of drug absorption by approximately 25% and 9%, respectively, but LDL-C reduction and HDL-C elevation are similar when atorvastatin is given with and without food. Atorvastatin is extensively metabolized to ortho- and para-hydroxylated derivatives by cytochrome P-450 3A4 (CYP 3A4) and to various beta-oxidation products, with approximately 70% of circulating inhibitory activity for HMG-CoA reductase attributed to active metabolites. Atorvastatin is primarily eliminated in bile following hepatic and/or extrahepatic metabolism, with a mean plasma elimination half-life of approximately 14 hours, but the half-life for inhibitory activity for HMG-CoA reductase is 20 to 30 hours due to the contribution of longer-lived active metabolites. Plasma concentrations of atorvastatin are higher in healthy elderly subjects compared with younger individuals, but LDL-C reduction is comparable to that seen in younger patient populations. Additionally, plasma concentrations of atorvastatin are similar in black and white subjects, but markedly increased in patients with chronic alcoholic liver disease, and similar in patients with moderate renal insufficiency compared with patients with normal renal function.

Pharmacokinetics: Atorvastatin is rapidly absorbed after oral administration, with maximal plasma concentrations occurring within 1 to 2 hours, and its extent of absorption and plasma concentrations increase in proportion to the atorvastatin dose. The absolute bioavailability of atorvastatin is approximately 12%, and the systemic availability of HMG-CoA reductase inhibitory activity is approximately 30%, attributed to pre-systemic clearance in gastrointestinal mucosa and/or first-pass metabolism in the liver. Food decreases the rate and extent of drug absorption by approximately 25% and 9%, respectively, but LDL-C reduction and HDL-C elevation are similar when atorvastatin is given with and without food. Atorvastatin is extensively metabolized to ortho- and para-hydroxylated derivatives by cytochrome P-450 3A4 (CYP 3A4) and to various beta-oxidation products, with approximately 70% of circulating inhibitory activity for HMG-CoA reductase attributed to active metabolites. Atorvastatin is primarily eliminated in bile following hepatic and/or extrahepatic metabolism, with a mean plasma elimination half-life of approximately 14 hours, but the half-life for inhibitory activity for HMG-CoA reductase is 20 to 30 hours due to the contribution of longer-lived active metabolites. In special populations, plasma concentrations of atorvastatin are higher in healthy elderly subjects (approximately 40% for Cmax and 30% for AUC) compared with younger individuals, but LDL-C reduction is comparable to that seen in younger patient populations. Additionally, plasma concentrations of atorvastatin are similar in black and white subjects, but markedly increased (approximately 16-fold in Cmax and 11-fold in AUC) in patients with chronic alcoholic liver disease.

Pharmacodynamics: Atorvastatin is a synthetic lipid-lowering agent that selectively and competitively inhibits 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase, the enzyme catalyzing the conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate, an early and rate-limiting step in cholesterol biosynthesis. By inhibiting this enzyme, atorvastatin reduces plasma cholesterol and lipoprotein levels by decreasing cholesterol synthesis in the liver and increasing the number of hepatic low-density lipoprotein (LDL) receptors, leading to enhanced uptake and catabolism of LDL. Atorvastatin reduces LDL-cholesterol (LDL-C) and the number of LDL particles, as well as very low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol (VLDL-C), serum triglycerides (TG), and intermediate-density lipoproteins (IDL), while increasing high-density lipoprotein-cholesterol (HDL-C). The lowering of total cholesterol, LDL-C, and apolipoprotein B (apo B) has been shown to reduce the risk of cardiovascular events and mortality. Atorvastatin has been demonstrated to be effective in reducing levels of total cholesterol, LDL-C, apo B, and total TG, and raising HDL-C levels in various patient populations, including those with familial hypercholesterolemia, mixed dyslipidemia, and hypertriglyceridemia. The risk of coronary artery disease (CAD) is associated with elevated levels of total cholesterol, LDL-C, and decreased levels of HDL-C, and atorvastatin's effects on these lipoproteins are considered major contributors to its cardiovascular benefits. The onset of atorvastatin's effects is not explicitly stated, but its duration of action is likely to be several days, given its half-life of approximately 14 hours. Special population considerations include the potential for increased risk of pancreatitis in patients with high triglyceride levels, and the need for dose adjustment in patients with hepatic impairment.
Pregnancy Summary: M-ATORVASTATIN is contraindicated in pregnancy. The drug should be administered to women of childbearing age only when they are highly unlikely to conceive. If pregnancy occurs during treatment, the drug should be discontinued. Animal studies suggest potential fetal toxicity, including delayed development and reduced postnatal survival, with placental transfer of the drug observed in rats.
Breastfeeding Summary: Atorvastatin is contraindicated during breastfeeding. It is excreted in human milk, with concentrations similar to those in plasma. The potential effects on the nursing infant are not well established, but caution is advised due to the risk of adverse reactions, including liver enzyme elevations and muscle damage. Breastfeeding women should not use atorvastatin.

Pharmacokinetics: Atorvastatin is rapidly absorbed after oral administration, with maximal plasma concentrations occurring within 1 to 2 hours, and its extent of absorption and plasma concentrations increase in proportion to the atorvastatin dose. The absolute bioavailability of atorvastatin is approximately 12%, and the systemic availability of HMG-CoA reductase inhibitory activity is approximately 30%, attributed to pre-systemic clearance in gastrointestinal mucosa and/or first-pass metabolism in the liver. Food decreases the rate and extent of drug absorption by approximately 25% and 9%, respectively, but LDL-C reduction and HDL-C elevation are similar when atorvastatin is given with and without food. Atorvastatin is extensively metabolized to ortho- and para-hydroxylated derivatives by cytochrome P-450 3A4 (CYP 3A4) and to various beta-oxidation products, with approximately 70% of circulating inhibitory activity for HMG-CoA reductase attributed to active metabolites. Atorvastatin is primarily eliminated in bile following hepatic and/or extrahepatic metabolism, with a mean plasma elimination half-life of approximately 14 hours, but the half-life for inhibitory activity for HMG-CoA reductase is 20 to 30 hours due to the contribution of longer-lived active metabolites. In special populations, plasma concentrations of atorvastatin are higher in healthy elderly subjects, and in patients with chronic alcoholic liver disease, while plasma concentrations and LDL-C lowering efficacy are similar in patients with moderate renal insufficiency.

Pharmacodynamics: Atorvastatin is a synthetic lipid-lowering agent that selectively and competitively inhibits 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase, the enzyme responsible for converting HMG-CoA to mevalonate, an early and rate-limiting step in cholesterol biosynthesis. By inhibiting this enzyme, atorvastatin reduces plasma cholesterol and lipoprotein levels by decreasing cholesterol synthesis in the liver and increasing the number of hepatic low-density lipoprotein (LDL) receptors on the cell surface for enhanced uptake and catabolism of LDL. Atorvastatin reduces LDL-cholesterol (LDL-C) and the number of LDL particles, as well as very low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol (VLDL-C), serum triglycerides (TG), and intermediate-density lipoproteins (IDL), while increasing high-density lipoprotein-cholesterol (HDL-C). Elevated serum cholesterol due to elevated LDL-C is a major risk factor for cardiovascular disease, and low serum concentration of HDL-C is also an independent risk factor. The lowering of total cholesterol, LDL-C, and apolipoprotein B (apo B) has been shown to reduce the risk of cardiovascular events and mortality. Atorvastatin has been demonstrated to be effective in reducing levels of total cholesterol, LDL-C, apo B, and total TG, and raising HDL-C levels in various patient populations, including those with familial hypercholesterolemia, non-familial forms of hypercholesterolemia, mixed dyslipidemia, hypertriglyceridemia, and dysbetalipoproteinemia. The onset of action for atorvastatin is not explicitly stated, but its effects are generally seen within a few weeks of treatment. The duration of action is also not specified, but it is known to be a long-acting agent. Special population considerations for PD effects include age, as the efficacy of atorvastatin may be reduced in older adults, and organ impairment, as patients with liver or kidney disease may require dose adjustments.
Pregnancy Summary: M-ATORVASTATIN is contraindicated in pregnancy. There is no experience with its use in pregnant women, and it should be administered to women of childbearing age only when they are highly unlikely to conceive. If pregnancy occurs while taking M-ATORVASTATIN, the drug should be discontinued. Animal studies suggest that HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors may affect fetal development, with evidence of placental transfer and fetal toxicity observed in rats and rabbits at maternally toxic doses.
Breastfeeding Summary: Atorvastatin is contraindicated during breastfeeding due to potential harm to the nursing infant. Atorvastatin is excreted in human milk, with concentrations similar to those in plasma. Potential effects on the nursing infant include unknown effects on growth and sexual maturation, and no effect on menstrual cycle was observed. Recommendations for breastfeeding women include avoiding use of atorvastatin.

Additionally, atorvastatin improves endothelial dysfunction in patients with type II hyperlipidemia, as evidenced by improved flow-mediated endothelium-dependent dilatation. The pharmacodynamic effects of atorvastatin are consistent across various patient populations, including those with mixed dyslipidemia, hypertriglyceridemia, and dysbetalipoproteinemia.

Pharmacokinetics: Atorvastatin calcium is rapidly absorbed after oral administration, with maximal plasma concentrations occurring within 1 to 2 hours, and its extent of absorption and plasma concentrations increase in proportion to the dose. The absolute bioavailability of atorvastatin calcium is approximately 12%, and the systemic availability of HMG-CoA reductase inhibitory activity is approximately 30%, attributed to presystemic clearance in gastrointestinal mucosa and/or first-pass metabolism in the liver. Food decreases the rate and extent of drug absorption by approximately 25% and 9%, respectively, but does not significantly affect LDL-C reduction and HDL-C elevation. Plasma atorvastatin concentrations are lower (approximately 30% for Cmax and AUC) following evening administration compared to morning dosing, but LDL-C reduction and HDL-C elevation are similar regardless of the time of administration. Atorvastatin is extensively bound to plasma proteins (≥98%), with a mean volume of distribution of approximately 381 liters, and poor penetration into red blood cells. It is primarily eliminated by biliary excretion, with a mean plasma elimination half-life of approximately 14 hours, but the half-life for inhibitory activity for HMG-CoA reductase is 20 to 30 hours due to the contribution of longer-lived active metabolites. Approximately 70% of circulating inhibitory activity for HMG-CoA reductase is attributed to active metabolites, which are formed through cytochrome P-450 3A4 (CYP 3A4) and beta-oxidation pathways. Atorvastatin is a substrate of the hepatic transporters OATP1B1 and OATP1B3, and the efflux transporters MDR1 and BCRP, which may limit intestinal absorption and biliary clearance. In special populations, plasma concentrations of atorvastatin are higher in healthy elderly subjects (approximately 40% for Cmax and 30% for AUC) and in patients with chronic alcoholic liver disease (approximately 16-fold in Cmax and 11-fold in AUC), but LDL-C reduction is comparable to that seen in younger patient populations. In patients with moderate renal insufficiency, plasma concentrations and LDL-C lowering efficacy of atorvastatin calcium are similar to those with normal renal function, but the lowest dose should be used as a precautionary measure.

Pharmacodynamics: Atorvastatin calcium, a synthetic lipid-lowering agent, exerts its pharmacodynamic effects by selectively and competitively inhibiting 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase, an enzyme catalyzing the conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate, a crucial step in cholesterol biosynthesis. This inhibition leads to a decrease in cholesterol synthesis in the liver and an increase in the number of hepatic low-density lipoprotein (LDL) receptors, resulting in enhanced uptake and catabolism of LDL. Consequently, atorvastatin calcium reduces LDL-cholesterol (LDL-C) and the number of LDL particles, while also lowering very low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol (VLDL-C), serum triglycerides (TG), and intermediate-density lipoproteins (IDL). Furthermore, it increases high-density lipoprotein-cholesterol (HDL-C) levels. The reduction in LDL-C and TG, and the increase in HDL-C, have been associated with a decreased risk of cardiovascular events and mortality. Atorvastatin calcium has been shown to be effective in various patient populations, including those with familial hypercholesterolemia, mixed dyslipidemia, and hypertriglyceridemia, and has been demonstrated to reduce the risk of coronary artery disease (CAD) by lowering total cholesterol, LDL-C, and apoB levels, and raising HDL-C levels. The pharmacodynamic effects of atorvastatin calcium are consistent with the established risk factors for CAD, including high LDL-C, low HDL-C, and high plasma TG.
Pregnancy Summary: MINT-ATORVASTATIN (atorvastatin calcium) is contraindicated during pregnancy. The drug should be administered to women of childbearing age only when they are highly unlikely to conceive and have been informed of the potential hazards. If pregnancy occurs while taking MINT-ATORVASTATIN, the drug should be discontinued. Animal studies suggest fetal toxicity and delayed development in rats and rabbits at maternally toxic doses. There is no experience with the drug in human pregnancy.
Breastfeeding Summary: MINT-ATORVASTATIN (atorvastatin calcium) is contraindicated during breastfeeding. The drug is excreted in human milk. Potential effects on the nursing infant include unknown effects due to limited data, but caution is advised due to the potential for adverse reactions. Recommendations for breastfeeding women include not breastfeeding while taking MINT-ATORVASTATIN.

Pharmacokinetics: Atorvastatin calcium is rapidly absorbed after oral administration, with maximal plasma concentrations occurring within 1 to 2 hours, and its extent of absorption and plasma concentrations increase in proportion to the dose. The absolute bioavailability of atorvastatin calcium is approximately 12%, and the systemic availability of HMG-CoA reductase inhibitory activity is approximately 30%, attributed to presystemic clearance in gastrointestinal mucosa and/or first-pass metabolism in the liver. Food decreases the rate and extent of drug absorption by approximately 25% and 9%, respectively, but LDL-C reduction and HDL-C elevation are similar when atorvastatin calcium is given with and without food. Plasma atorvastatin concentrations are lower (approximately 30% for Cmax and AUC) following drug administration in the evening compared with morning dosing, but LDL-C reduction and HDL-C elevation are the same regardless of the time of drug administration. Atorvastatin is extensively bound to plasma proteins (≥98%), with a mean volume of distribution of approximately 381 liters, and it is poorly distributed into red blood cells. Atorvastatin is extensively metabolized to ortho- and para-hydroxylated derivatives by cytochrome P-450 3A4 (CYP 3A4) and to various beta-oxidation products, with approximately 70% of circulating inhibitory activity for HMG-CoA reductase attributed to active metabolites. Atorvastatin and its metabolites are eliminated by biliary excretion, with a mean plasma elimination half-life of approximately 14 hours, but the half-life for inhibitory activity for HMG-CoA reductase is 20 to 30 hours due to the contribution of longer-lived active metabolites. Less than 2% of a dose of atorvastatin is recovered in urine following oral administration. In special populations, plasma concentrations of atorvastatin are higher in healthy elderly subjects (approximately 40% for Cmax and 30% for AUC) compared with younger individuals, but LDL-C reduction is comparable to that seen in younger patient populations. Plasma concentrations of atorvastatin are similar in black and white subjects, but markedly increased (approximately 16-fold in Cmax and 11-fold in AUC) in patients with chronic alcoholic liver disease. In patients with moderate renal insufficiency, plasma concentrations and LDL-C lowering efficacy of atorvastatin calcium are similar to those in patients with normal renal function, but the lowest dose (10 mg/day) should be used in these patients, and similar precautions apply in patients with severe renal insufficiency.

Pharmacodynamics: Atorvastatin calcium is a synthetic lipid-lowering agent that selectively and competitively inhibits 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase, an enzyme catalyzing the conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate, an early and rate-limiting step in cholesterol biosynthesis. By inhibiting this enzyme, atorvastatin calcium reduces cholesterol synthesis in the liver and increases the number of hepatic low-density lipoprotein (LDL) receptors on the cell surface, leading to enhanced uptake and catabolism of LDL. This results in decreased levels of LDL-cholesterol (LDL-C), very low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol (VLDL-C), serum triglycerides (TG), and intermediate-density lipoproteins (IDL), as well as increased levels of high-density lipoprotein-cholesterol (HDL-C). The lowering of total cholesterol, LDL-C, and apoB has been shown to reduce the risk of cardiovascular events and mortality. Atorvastatin calcium has been demonstrated to be effective in reducing levels of total cholesterol, LDL-C, apoB, and total TG, and raising HDL-C levels in various patient populations, including those with familial hypercholesterolemia, mixed dyslipidemia, and hypertriglyceridemia. The reduction of LDL-C and TG, while simultaneously increasing HDL-C, has been associated with decreased cardiovascular risk, and effective treatment of hypercholesterolemia/dyslipidemia has consistently been shown to reduce the risk of coronary artery disease.
Pregnancy Summary: MINT-ATORVASTATIN (atorvastatin calcium) is contraindicated during pregnancy. There is no experience with its use in pregnant women. Animal studies suggest potential fetal toxicity, including delayed development and reduced post-natal survival. If pregnancy occurs during treatment, the drug should be discontinued and the patient informed of the potential risk to the fetus.
Breastfeeding Summary: Atorvastatin calcium is contraindicated during breastfeeding. It is excreted in human milk, and the potential for adverse reactions in nursing infants exists. No effects on growth or sexual maturation in pediatric patients have been reported, but adolescent females should be counseled on appropriate contraceptive methods while on therapy. Discontinue breastfeeding.

Pharmacokinetics: Atorvastatin is rapidly absorbed after oral administration, with maximal plasma concentrations occurring within 1 to 2 hours, and its extent of absorption and plasma concentrations increase in proportion to atorvastatin dose. The absolute bioavailability of atorvastatin is approximately 12%, and the systemic availability of HMG-CoA reductase inhibitory activity is approximately 30%, attributed to presystemic clearance in gastrointestinal mucosa and/or first-pass metabolism in the liver. Food decreases the rate and extent of drug absorption by approximately 25% and 9%, respectively, but LDL-C reduction and HDL-C elevation are similar when atorvastatin is given with and without food. Atorvastatin is extensively metabolized to ortho- and para-hydroxylated derivatives by cytochrome P-450 3A4 (CYP 3A4) and to various beta-oxidation products, with approximately 70% of circulating inhibitory activity for HMG-CoA reductase attributed to active metabolites. Atorvastatin is primarily eliminated in bile following hepatic and/or extrahepatic metabolism, with a mean plasma elimination half-life of approximately 14 hours, but the half-life for inhibitory activity for HMG-CoA reductase is 20 to 30 hours due to the contribution of longer-lived active metabolites. Less than 2% of a dose of atorvastatin is recovered in urine following oral administration. In special populations, plasma concentrations of atorvastatin are higher in healthy elderly subjects (approximately 40% for Cmax and 30% for AUC) and in patients with chronic alcoholic liver disease (approximately 16-fold in Cmax and 11-fold in AUC), while plasma concentrations and LDL-C lowering efficacy are similar in patients with moderate renal insufficiency compared with patients with normal renal function.

Pharmacodynamics: Atorvastatin calcium is a synthetic lipid-lowering agent that selectively and competitively inhibits 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase, an enzyme catalyzing the conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate, an early and rate-limiting step in cholesterol biosynthesis. By inhibiting this enzyme, atorvastatin calcium reduces plasma cholesterol and lipoprotein levels by decreasing cholesterol synthesis in the liver and increasing the number of hepatic low-density lipoprotein (LDL) receptors on the cell surface for enhanced uptake and catabolism of LDL. Atorvastatin calcium also reduces very low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol (VLDL-C), serum triglycerides (TG), and intermediate-density lipoproteins (IDL), while increasing high-density lipoprotein-cholesterol (HDL-C). The lowering of total cholesterol, LDL-C, and apoB has been shown to reduce the risk of cardiovascular events and mortality. Atorvastatin calcium has been demonstrated to be effective in reducing levels of total cholesterol, LDL-C, apoB, and total TG, and raising HDL-C levels in various patient populations, including those with familial hypercholesterolemia, mixed dyslipidemia, hypertriglyceridemia, and dysbetalipoproteinemia. The reduction of LDL-C and the number of LDL particles, as well as the lowering of VLDL-C, TG, and IDL, are associated with decreased risk of coronary artery disease (CAD), while elevated HDL-C levels are associated with decreased cardiovascular risk. The onset of action for atorvastatin calcium is not explicitly stated, but its effects on lipid profiles are typically observed within a few weeks of treatment initiation. The duration of action is also not specified, but atorvastatin calcium is known to have a long half-life, allowing for once-daily dosing. Special population considerations include the potential for increased risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis in patients with renal impairment, and the need for dose adjustment in patients with hepatic impairment.
Pregnancy Summary: Atorvastatin is contraindicated in pregnancy. There is no experience with atorvastatin in human pregnancy, but animal studies suggest potential fetal toxicity. If pregnancy occurs during treatment, the drug should be discontinued. The most dangerous trimester is not specified, but animal studies indicate potential placental transfer and fetal toxicity.
Breastfeeding Summary: Atorvastatin is contraindicated during breastfeeding. It is excreted in human milk, and potential effects on the nursing infant include unknown effects due to lack of controlled clinical trials in lactating women. There is no information on effects on milk production/supply. Recommendations for breastfeeding women include not breastfeeding while taking atorvastatin.

Pharmacokinetics: Atorvastatin is rapidly absorbed after oral administration, with maximal plasma concentrations occurring within 1 to 2 hours, and its extent of absorption and plasma concentrations increase in proportion to atorvastatin dose. The absolute bioavailability of atorvastatin is approximately 12%, and the systemic availability of HMG-CoA reductase inhibitory activity is approximately 30%, primarily due to presystemic clearance in gastrointestinal mucosa and/or first-pass metabolism in the liver. Food decreases the rate and extent of drug absorption by approximately 25% and 9%, respectively, but LDL-C reduction and HDL-C elevation are similar when atorvastatin is given with and without food. Atorvastatin is extensively metabolized to ortho- and para-hydroxylated derivatives by cytochrome P-450 3A4 (CYP 3A4) and to various beta-oxidation products, with approximately 70% of circulating inhibitory activity for HMG-CoA reductase attributed to active metabolites. Atorvastatin is primarily eliminated in bile following hepatic and/or extrahepatic metabolism, with a mean plasma elimination half-life of approximately 14 hours, but the half-life for inhibitory activity for HMG-CoA reductase is 20 to 30 hours due to the contribution of longer-lived active metabolites. In special populations, plasma concentrations of atorvastatin are higher in healthy elderly subjects (approximately 40% for Cmax and 30% for AUC) and in patients with chronic alcoholic liver disease (approximately 16-fold in Cmax and 11-fold in AUC), while plasma concentrations and LDL-C lowering efficacy are similar in patients with moderate renal insufficiency compared with patients with normal renal function.

Pharmacodynamics: Atorvastatin calcium is a synthetic lipid-lowering agent that selectively and competitively inhibits 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase, an enzyme catalyzing the conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate, an early and rate-limiting step in cholesterol biosynthesis. By inhibiting this enzyme, atorvastatin calcium reduces plasma cholesterol and lipoprotein levels by decreasing cholesterol synthesis in the liver and increasing the number of hepatic Low-Density Lipoprotein (LDL) receptors on the cell surface for enhanced uptake and catabolism of LDL. Atorvastatin calcium lowers LDL-Cholesterol (LDL-C) and the number of LDL particles, reduces Very Low-Density Lipoprotein-Cholesterol (VLDL-C), serum triglycerides (TG), and Intermediate Density Lipoproteins (IDL), while increasing High Density Lipoprotein-Cholesterol (HDL-C). The lowering of total cholesterol, LDL-C, and ApoB has been shown to reduce the risk of cardiovascular events and mortality. Atorvastatin calcium has been demonstrated to be effective in reducing levels of total cholesterol, LDL-C, apoB, and total TG, and raising HDL-C levels in various patient populations, including those with familial hypercholesterolemia, non-familial forms of hypercholesterolemia, mixed dyslipidemia, hypertriglyceridemia, and dysbetalipoproteinemia. The clinical effects of atorvastatin calcium are associated with a reduction in the risk of coronary artery disease (CAD), and its use has been consistently shown to reduce the risk of CAD, regardless of the intervention used. The onset of action of atorvastatin calcium is not explicitly stated, but its effects are generally seen within a few weeks of treatment, with a duration of action that can last for several days after discontinuation. Special population considerations include the potential for increased risk of pancreatitis in patients with high triglyceride levels, and the need for dose adjustment in patients with hepatic impairment.
Pregnancy Summary: Atorvastatin is contraindicated in pregnancy. There is no experience with its use in pregnant women, but animal studies suggest potential fetal toxicity. If pregnancy occurs during treatment, the drug should be discontinued. The most dangerous trimester is not specified, but animal studies indicate potential placental transfer and fetal toxicity. Fetal/neonatal risks mentioned include delayed development, post-natal survival reduction, and potential malformations.
Breastfeeding Summary: Atorvastatin calcium is contraindicated during breastfeeding. Atorvastatin is excreted in human milk, and its presence in milk may cause adverse reactions in nursing infants. Potential effects on the nursing infant include unknown effects on growth and sexual maturation, and the effects on menstrual cycle were not assessed. Recommendations for breastfeeding women include avoiding use of atorvastatin calcium.

Pharmacokinetics: Atorvastatin is rapidly absorbed after oral administration, with maximal plasma concentrations occurring within 1 to 2 hours, and its extent of absorption and plasma concentrations increase in proportion to the atorvastatin dose. The absolute bioavailability of atorvastatin is approximately 12%, while the systemic availability of HMG-CoA reductase inhibitory activity is approximately 30%, attributed to pre-systemic clearance in gastrointestinal mucosa and/or first-pass metabolism in the liver. Food decreases the rate and extent of drug absorption by approximately 25% and 9%, respectively, but LDL-C reduction and HDL-C elevation are similar when atorvastatin is given with and without food. The mean volume of distribution of atorvastatin is approximately 381 liters, and it is ≥98% bound to plasma proteins, indicating poor drug penetration into red blood cells. Atorvastatin is extensively metabolized to ortho- and para-hydroxylated derivatives by cytochrome P-450 3A4 (CYP 3A4) and to various beta-oxidation products, with approximately 70% of circulating inhibitory activity for HMG-CoA reductase attributed to active metabolites. Atorvastatin and its metabolites are eliminated by biliary excretion, with a mean plasma elimination half-life of approximately 14 hours, but the half-life for inhibitory activity for HMG-CoA reductase is 20 to 30 hours due to the contribution of longer-lived active metabolites. In special populations, plasma concentrations of atorvastatin are higher in healthy elderly subjects (approximately 40% for Cmax and 30% for AUC) compared with younger individuals, but LDL-C reduction is comparable to that seen in younger patient populations. In patients with chronic alcoholic liver disease, plasma concentrations of atorvastatin are markedly increased (approximately 16-fold in Cmax and 11-fold in AUC), and in patients with severe renal insufficiency, the lowest dosage should be used and implemented cautiously.

Pharmacodynamics: Atorvastatin, a synthetic lipid-lowering agent, exerts its pharmacodynamic effects by selectively and competitively inhibiting 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase, an enzyme catalyzing the conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate, a rate-limiting step in cholesterol biosynthesis. By inhibiting this enzyme, atorvastatin reduces plasma cholesterol and lipoprotein levels by decreasing cholesterol synthesis in the liver and increasing the number of hepatic Low Density Lipoprotein (LDL) receptors, leading to enhanced uptake and catabolism of LDL. Atorvastatin reduces LDL-Cholesterol (LDL-C) and the number of LDL particles, lowers Very Low Density Lipoprotein-Cholesterol (VLDL-C) and serum triglycerides, reduces the number of apolipoprotein B (apo B) containing particles, and increases High Density Lipoprotein-Cholesterol (HDL-C). The lowering of total cholesterol, LDL-C, and apo B has been shown to reduce the risk of cardiovascular events and mortality. Atorvastatin is effective in reducing LDL-C in patients with various forms of hypercholesterolemia, including homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, and also improves endothelial dysfunction in patients with type II hyperlipidemia. The onset of action is rapid, with maximal plasma concentrations occurring within 1-2 hours, and the duration of action is sustained, with similar LDL-C reduction and HDL-C elevation regardless of food intake or time of administration.
Pregnancy Summary: Atorvastatin is contraindicated in pregnancy. The drug has no experience in human pregnancy, but animal studies suggest potential fetal toxicity and delayed development. If pregnancy occurs during treatment, atorvastatin should be discontinued and the patient informed of the potential risk to the fetus.
Breastfeeding Summary: Atorvastatin is contraindicated during breastfeeding. Atorvastatin is excreted in human milk, with concentrations similar to those in plasma. Potential effects on the nursing infant include unknown effects on growth and sexual maturation, and no effect on menstrual cycle was observed. No effects on milk production/supply were mentioned. Recommendations for breastfeeding women include avoiding use of atorvastatin.

Pharmacokinetics: Atorvastatin is rapidly absorbed after oral administration, with maximal plasma concentrations occurring within 1 to 2 hours, and its extent of absorption and plasma concentrations increase in proportion to the atorvastatin dose. The absolute bioavailability of atorvastatin is approximately 12%, and the systemic availability of HMG-CoA reductase inhibitory activity is approximately 30%, attributed to pre-systemic clearance in gastrointestinal mucosa and/or first-pass metabolism in the liver. Food decreases the rate and extent of drug absorption by approximately 25% and 9%, but LDL-C reduction and HDL-C elevation are similar when atorvastatin is given with and without food. Plasma atorvastatin concentrations are lower following evening administration compared to morning dosing, but LDL-C reduction and HDL-C elevation are the same regardless of the time of drug administration. Atorvastatin is extensively bound to plasma proteins, with a mean volume of distribution of approximately 381 liters, and it is primarily eliminated in bile following hepatic and/or extrahepatic metabolism, with a mean plasma elimination half-life of approximately 14 hours. However, the half-life for inhibitory activity for HMG-CoA reductase is 20 to 30 hours due to the contribution of longer-lived active metabolites. In special populations, plasma concentrations of atorvastatin are higher in healthy elderly subjects, and in patients with chronic alcoholic liver disease, but its LDL-C lowering efficacy is comparable in these populations. Additionally, plasma concentrations and LDL-C lowering efficacy of atorvastatin are similar in patients with moderate renal insufficiency compared to patients with normal renal function, but the lowest dose should be used in these patients.

Pharmacodynamics: Atorvastatin, a synthetic lipid-lowering agent, exerts its pharmacodynamic effects by selectively and competitively inhibiting 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme in cholesterol biosynthesis. This inhibition reduces the conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate, thereby decreasing cholesterol synthesis in the liver and increasing the number of hepatic Low Density Lipoprotein (LDL) receptors, leading to enhanced uptake and catabolism of LDL. As a result, atorvastatin lowers plasma cholesterol and lipoprotein levels, reducing LDL-Cholesterol (LDL-C) and the number of LDL particles, while also lowering Very Low Density Lipoprotein-Cholesterol (VLDL-C), serum triglycerides, and Intermediate Density Lipoproteins (IDL), and increasing High Density Lipoprotein-Cholesterol (HDL-C). The reduction in LDL-C and the increase in HDL-C have been shown to reduce the risk of cardiovascular events and mortality. Atorvastatin is effective in reducing LDL-C in patients with various forms of hypercholesterolemia, including homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, and has also been shown to improve endothelial dysfunction in patients with type II hyperlipidemia. The pharmacodynamic effects of atorvastatin are consistent across different patient populations, including those with dysbetalipoproteinemia and metabolic syndrome, and are not significantly affected by food or the time of administration.
Pregnancy Summary: Atorvastatin is contraindicated in pregnancy. The drug should be administered to women of childbearing age only when they are highly unlikely to conceive and have been informed of the potential hazards. If pregnancy occurs while taking atorvastatin, the drug should be discontinued. Animal studies suggest fetal toxicity, delayed development, and reduced post-natal survival in rats exposed to high doses of atorvastatin.
Breastfeeding Summary: Atorvastatin is contraindicated during breastfeeding. Atorvastatin is excreted in human milk, with concentrations similar to those in plasma. The potential effects on the nursing infant are unknown. However, caution is advised due to the risk of muscle toxicity and potential effects on liver enzymes. Recommendations include avoiding use or discontinuing breastfeeding.

Pharmacokinetics: Atorvastatin is rapidly absorbed after oral administration, with maximal plasma concentrations occurring within 1 to 2 hours, and its extent of absorption and plasma concentrations increase in proportion to the atorvastatin dose. The absolute bioavailability of atorvastatin is approximately 12%, and the systemic availability of HMG-CoA reductase inhibitory activity is approximately 30%, attributed to presystemic clearance in the gastrointestinal mucosa and/or first-pass metabolism in the liver. Food decreases the rate and extent of drug absorption by approximately 25% and 9%, respectively, but LDL-C reduction and HDL-C elevation are similar when atorvastatin is given with and without food. Atorvastatin is extensively bound to plasma proteins, with a mean volume of distribution of approximately 381 liters, and is poorly distributed into red blood cells. The drug is extensively metabolized to ortho- and para-hydroxylated derivatives by cytochrome P-450 3A4 (CYP 3A4) and to various beta-oxidation products, with approximately 70% of circulating inhibitory activity for HMG-CoA reductase attributed to active metabolites. Atorvastatin is eliminated primarily in bile following hepatic and/or extrahepatic metabolism, with a mean plasma elimination half-life of approximately 14 hours, but the half-life for inhibitory activity for HMG-CoA reductase is 20 to 30 hours due to the contribution of longer-lived active metabolites. In special populations, plasma concentrations of atorvastatin are higher in healthy elderly subjects (approximately 40% for Cmax and 30% for AUC) compared with younger individuals, and in patients with chronic alcoholic liver disease (approximately 16-fold in Cmax and 11-fold in AUC). In contrast, plasma concentrations of atorvastatin are similar in black and white subjects, and in patients with moderate renal insufficiency compared with patients with normal renal function.

Pharmacodynamics: Atorvastatin calcium is a synthetic lipid-lowering agent that acts as a selective, competitive inhibitor of 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase, an enzyme catalyzing the conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate, a rate-limiting step in cholesterol biosynthesis. By inhibiting this enzyme, atorvastatin calcium reduces cholesterol synthesis in the liver and increases the number of hepatic Low Density Lipoprotein (LDL) receptors on the cell surface, enhancing the uptake and catabolism of LDL. This results in decreased levels of LDL-Cholesterol (LDL-C) and the number of LDL particles, as well as reduced levels of Very Low Density Lipoprotein-Cholesterol (VLDL-C), serum triglycerides, and Intermediate Density Lipoproteins (IDL). Additionally, atorvastatin calcium increases High Density Lipoprotein-Cholesterol (HDL-C) levels. The lowering of total cholesterol, LDL-C, and ApoB has been shown to reduce the risk of cardiovascular events and mortality. Atorvastatin calcium has been demonstrated to be effective in reducing levels of total cholesterol, LDL-C, apoB, and total triglycerides, and raising HDL-C levels in various patient populations, including those with familial and non-familial forms of hypercholesterolemia, mixed dyslipidemia, hypertriglyceridemia, and dysbetalipoproteinemia. The reduction of LDL-C and the number of LDL particles, as well as the lowering of VLDL-C and serum triglycerides, are associated with decreased risk of coronary artery disease (CAD), while increased HDL-C levels are associated with decreased cardiovascular risk. The total cholesterol to HDL-C ratio (TC:HDL-C) is considered the best predictor of CAD, and effective treatment of hypercholesterolemia/dyslipidemia has consistently been shown to reduce the risk of CAD, regardless of the intervention used.
Pregnancy Summary: Atorvastatin is contraindicated in pregnancy. There is no experience with its use in pregnant women, but animal studies suggest fetal toxicity, delayed development, and reduced post-natal survival at maternally toxic doses. If pregnancy occurs during treatment, the drug should be discontinued, and the patient informed of the potential risk to the fetus.
Breastfeeding Summary: Atorvastatin is contraindicated during breastfeeding due to potential adverse reactions in nursing infants. Atorvastatin is excreted in human milk, with concentrations similar to those in plasma. There is a potential risk of effects on the nursing infant, including gastrointestinal and musculoskeletal disorders. Breastfeeding women should not take atorvastatin.

Pharmacokinetics: Atorvastatin is rapidly absorbed after oral administration, with maximal plasma concentrations occurring within 1 to 2 hours, and its extent of absorption and plasma concentrations increase in proportion to atorvastatin dose. The absolute bioavailability of atorvastatin is approximately 12%, and the systemic availability of HMG-CoA reductase inhibitory activity is approximately 30%, attributed to pre-systemic clearance in gastrointestinal mucosa and/or first-pass metabolism in the liver. Food decreases the rate and extent of drug absorption by approximately 25% and 9%, as assessed by Cmax and AUC respectively, but LDL-C reduction and HDL-C elevation are similar when atorvastatin is given with and without food. Plasma atorvastatin concentrations are lower (approximately 30% for Cmax and AUC) following drug administration in the evening compared with morning dosing, but LDL-C reduction and HDL-C elevation are the same regardless of the time of drug administration. Atorvastatin is extensively bound to plasma proteins, with a mean volume of distribution of approximately 381 liters, and it is primarily eliminated in bile following hepatic and/or extrahepatic metabolism, with a mean plasma elimination half-life of approximately 14 hours. However, the half-life for inhibitory activity for HMG-CoA reductase is 20 to 30 hours due to the contribution of longer-lived active metabolites. Approximately 70% of circulating inhibitory activity for HMG-CoA reductase is attributed to active metabolites, which are formed through cytochrome P-450 3A4 (CYP 3A4) and beta-oxidation pathways. Atorvastatin is a substrate of the hepatic transporters, organic anion-transporting polypeptide 1B1 (OATP1B1) and 1B3 (OATP1B3) transporter, and its metabolites are substrates of OATP1B1. In special populations, plasma concentrations of atorvastatin are higher in healthy elderly subjects (approximately 40% for Cmax and 30% for AUC) compared with younger individuals, but LDL-C reduction is comparable to that seen in younger patient populations. In patients with chronic alcoholic liver disease (Childs-Pugh B), plasma concentrations of atorvastatin are markedly increased (approximately 16-fold in Cmax and 11-fold in AUC), and in patients with moderate renal insufficiency, plasma concentrations and LDL-C lowering efficacy of atorvastatin are similar to those in patients with normal renal function.

Pharmacodynamics: Atorvastatin, a synthetic lipid-lowering agent, exerts its pharmacodynamic effects by selectively and competitively inhibiting 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme in cholesterol biosynthesis. This inhibition reduces the conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate, thereby lowering plasma cholesterol and lipoprotein levels. Atorvastatin increases the number of hepatic Low Density Lipoprotein (LDL) receptors, enhancing the uptake and catabolism of LDL. Consequently, it reduces LDL-Cholesterol (LDL-C) and the number of LDL particles, while also lowering Very Low Density Lipoprotein-Cholesterol (VLDL-C), serum triglycerides, and Intermediate Density Lipoproteins (IDL). Notably, atorvastatin increases High Density Lipoprotein-Cholesterol (HDL-C) levels. The reduction of LDL-C, VLDL-C, and triglycerides, as well as the increase in HDL-C, have been shown to reduce the risk of cardiovascular events and mortality. Atorvastatin is effective in patients with various forms of hypercholesterolemia, including homozygous and heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, mixed dyslipidemia, and dysbetalipoproteinemia. Additionally, it has been shown to improve endothelial dysfunction in patients with type II hyperlipidemia. The onset of action for atorvastatin is rapid, with maximal plasma concentrations occurring within 1-2 hours, and the duration of action is sustained, with LDL-C reduction and HDL-C elevation observed regardless of the time of drug administration. The pharmacodynamic effects of atorvastatin are not significantly affected by food or the time of day, although food may decrease the rate and extent of drug absorption by approximately 25% and 9%, respectively.
Pregnancy Summary: RIVA-ATORVASTATIN is contraindicated during pregnancy. There is no experience with the drug in pregnant women, and it should be administered to women of childbearing age only when they are highly unlikely to conceive. If pregnancy occurs while taking RIVA-ATORVASTATIN, the drug should be discontinued. Animal studies suggest potential fetal toxicity, including delayed development and reduced postnatal survival.
Breastfeeding Summary: Atorvastatin is contraindicated during breastfeeding. The drug is excreted in human milk, and its presence in milk may cause adverse reactions in nursing infants. Potential effects on the nursing infant include unknown effects on growth and sexual maturation. Women taking atorvastatin should not breastfeed.

Pharmacokinetics: Atorvastatin is rapidly absorbed after oral administration, with maximal plasma concentrations occurring within 1 to 2 hours, and its extent of absorption and plasma concentrations increase in proportion to the atorvastatin dose. The absolute bioavailability of atorvastatin is approximately 12%, while the systemic availability of HMG-CoA reductase inhibitory activity is approximately 30%, attributed to pre-systemic clearance in gastrointestinal mucosa and/or first-pass metabolism in the liver. Food decreases the rate and extent of drug absorption by approximately 25% and 9%, respectively, but LDL-C reduction and HDL-C elevation are similar when atorvastatin is given with and without food. Plasma atorvastatin concentrations are lower (approximately 30% for Cmax and AUC) following drug administration in the evening compared with morning dosing, but LDL-C reduction and HDL-C elevation are the same regardless of the time of drug administration. Atorvastatin is extensively bound to plasma proteins (≥98%) and has a mean volume of distribution of approximately 381 liters, indicating poor penetration into red blood cells. The drug is extensively metabolized to ortho- and para-hydroxylated derivatives by cytochrome P-450 3A4 (CYP 3A4) and to various beta-oxidation products, with approximately 70% of circulating inhibitory activity for HMG-CoA reductase attributed to active metabolites. Atorvastatin is eliminated primarily in bile following hepatic and/or extrahepatic metabolism, with a mean plasma elimination half-life of approximately 14 hours, but the half-life for inhibitory activity for HMG-CoA reductase is 20 to 30 hours due to the contribution of longer-lived active metabolites. Less than 2% of a dose of atorvastatin is recovered in urine following oral administration. In special populations, plasma concentrations of atorvastatin are higher in healthy elderly subjects (approximately 40% for Cmax and 30% for AUC) compared with younger individuals, but LDL-C reduction is comparable to that seen in younger patient populations. Plasma concentrations of atorvastatin in women differ (approximately 20% higher for Cmax and 10% lower for AUC) from those in men, but there is no clinically significant difference in LDL-C reduction between men and women. Plasma concentrations of atorvastatin are similar in black and white subjects, but are markedly increased (approximately 16-fold in Cmax and 11-fold in AUC) in patients with chronic alcoholic liver disease. In patients with moderate renal insufficiency, plasma concentrations and LDL-C lowering efficacy of atorvastatin calcium are similar to those in patients with normal renal function, but the lowest dose (10 mg/day) of Sandoz Atorvastatin should be used in these patients.

By inhibiting this enzyme, atorvastatin calcium reduces plasma cholesterol and lipoprotein levels by decreasing cholesterol synthesis in the liver and increasing the number of hepatic Low Density Lipoprotein (LDL) receptors on the cell surface for enhanced uptake and catabolism of LDL. This results in a reduction of LDL-Cholesterol (LDL-C) and the number of LDL particles, as well as a decrease in Very Low Density Lipoprotein-Cholesterol (VLDL-C), serum triglycerides (TG), and Intermediate Density Lipoproteins (IDL), and an increase in High Density Lipoprotein-Cholesterol (HDL-C). Atorvastatin calcium is effective in reducing LDL-C in patients with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, a condition that rarely responds to other lipid-lowering medications, and also reduces IDL-C and apolipoprotein E (apo E) in patients with dysbetalipoproteinemia (Type III). The onset of action of atorvastatin calcium is rapid, with maximal plasma concentrations occurring within 1-2 hours, and the duration of action is sustained, with LDL-C reduction and HDL-C elevation similar when administered with and without food. Atorvastatin calcium is approximately 95-99% bioavailable compared to solutions, with a low systemic availability attributed to presystemic clearance in gastrointestinal mucosa and/or first-pass metabolism in the liver. The mean volume of distribution of atorvastatin is approximately 381 liters, and it is ≥ 98% bound to plasma proteins. The pharmacodynamic effects of atorvastatin calcium are well established, with epidemiologic, clinical, and experimental studies demonstrating that high LDL-C, low HDL-C, and high plasma TG promote human atherosclerosis and are risk factors for developing cardiovascular disease. Pharmacokinetics: Atorvastatin is rapidly absorbed after oral administration, with maximal plasma concentrations occurring within 1 to 2 hours, and its extent of absorption and plasma concentrations increase in proportion to the atorvastatin dose. The absolute bioavailability of atorvastatin is approximately 12%, and the systemic availability of HMG-CoA reductase inhibitory activity is approximately 30%, attributed to presystemic clearance in gastrointestinal mucosa and/or first-pass metabolism in the liver. Food decreases the rate and extent of drug absorption by approximately 25% and 9%, respectively, but LDL-C reduction and HDL-C elevation are similar when atorvastatin is given with and without food. Atorvastatin is extensively metabolized to ortho- and para-hydroxylated derivatives by cytochrome P-450 3A4 (CYP 3A4) and to various beta-oxidation products, with approximately 70% of circulating inhibitory activity for HMG-CoA reductase attributed to active metabolites. Atorvastatin is primarily eliminated in bile following hepatic and/or extrahepatic metabolism, with a mean plasma elimination half-life of approximately 14 hours, but the half-life for inhibitory activity for HMG-CoA reductase is 20 to 30 hours due to the contribution of longer-lived active metabolites. The mean volume of distribution of atorvastatin is approximately 381 liters, and it is ≥98% bound to plasma proteins. Atorvastatin is a substrate of the hepatic transporters, organic anion-transporting polypeptide 1B1 (OATP1B1) and 1B3 (OATP1B3) transporter, and metabolites of atorvastatin are substrates of OATP1B1. Special population considerations include higher plasma concentrations in healthy elderly subjects (approximately 40% for Cmax and 30% for AUC) and in patients with chronic alcoholic liver disease (approximately 16-fold in Cmax and 11-fold in AUC), but similar LDL-C reduction in these populations. In pediatric patients, variability in atorvastatin PK is primarily affected by body weight, and allometric scaling by body weight is used to describe the changes in the apparent oral clearance of atorvastatin.

Pharmacodynamics: Atorvastatin calcium is a synthetic lipid-lowering agent that selectively and competitively inhibits 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase, an enzyme catalyzing the conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate, a rate-limiting step in cholesterol biosynthesis in the liver. By inhibiting this enzyme, atorvastatin calcium reduces plasma cholesterol and lipoprotein levels, including low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) cholesterol, and triglycerides, while increasing high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol. This is achieved through enhanced uptake and catabolism of LDL by increasing the number of hepatic LDL receptors on the cell surface. Atorvastatin calcium also reduces the number of LDL particles and apolipoprotein B (apo B) containing particles. The reduction in LDL cholesterol and apo B levels has been shown to decrease the risk of cardiovascular events and mortality. The drug's pharmacodynamic effects are evident in its ability to lower total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, and apo B, while raising HDL cholesterol levels. The IC50 of atorvastatin calcium for HMG-CoA reductase inhibition is not explicitly stated, but its efficacy in reducing cholesterol levels has been demonstrated in various clinical studies, including those involving patients with familial hypercholesterolemia, mixed dyslipidemia, and hypertriglyceridemia. The onset of action for atorvastatin calcium is not specified, but its effects on lipid profiles are typically observed within a few weeks of treatment. The duration of action is also not explicitly stated, but its lipid-lowering effects are sustained with continued treatment. Special population considerations include the potential for increased risk of pancreatitis in patients with high triglyceride levels, particularly if due to increased intermediate-density lipoproteins (IDL) or associated with decreased HDL or increased LDL cholesterol.
Pregnancy Summary: Atorvastatin calcium tablets are contraindicated in pregnancy due to the potential for fetal harm. The most dangerous trimester is the third trimester, where fetal risks include hypotension and neonatal renal failure. There is no information on specific malformations associated with atorvastatin use in pregnancy. If pregnancy occurs during treatment, the drug should be discontinued immediately and the patient referred to a specialist for further management.

Pharmacokinetics: Atorvastatin is rapidly absorbed after oral administration, with maximal plasma concentrations occurring within 1 to 2 hours, and its extent of absorption and plasma concentrations increase in proportion to the atorvastatin dose. The absolute bioavailability of atorvastatin is approximately 12%, and the systemic availability of HMG-CoA reductase inhibitory activity is approximately 30%, primarily due to presystemic clearance in gastrointestinal mucosa and/or first-pass metabolism in the liver. Food decreases the rate and extent of drug absorption by approximately 25% and 9%, respectively, but LDL-C reduction and HDL-C elevation are similar when atorvastatin is given with and without food. Atorvastatin is extensively metabolized to ortho- and para-hydroxylated derivatives by cytochrome P-450 3A4 (CYP 3A4) and to various beta-oxidation products, with approximately 70% of circulating inhibitory activity for HMG-CoA reductase attributed to active metabolites. Atorvastatin is primarily eliminated in bile following hepatic and/or extrahepatic metabolism, with a mean plasma elimination half-life of approximately 14 hours, but the half-life for inhibitory activity for HMG-CoA reductase is 20 to 30 hours due to the contribution of longer-lived active metabolites. Atorvastatin is approximately 98% bound to plasma proteins, and its mean volume of distribution is approximately 381 liters. In special populations, plasma concentrations of atorvastatin are higher in healthy elderly subjects (approximately 40% for Cmax and 30% for AUC) compared with younger individuals, but LDL-C reduction is comparable to that seen in younger patient populations. Plasma concentrations of atorvastatin are also similar in black and white subjects, but markedly increased (approximately 16-fold in Cmax and 11-fold in AUC) in patients with chronic alcoholic liver disease. In patients with moderate renal insufficiency, plasma concentrations and LDL-C lowering efficacy of atorvastatin calcium are similar to those in patients with normal renal function, but the lowest dose should be used as a precautionary measure.

Pharmacodynamics: Atorvastatin calcium is a synthetic lipid-lowering agent that exerts its pharmacodynamic effects by selectively and competitively inhibiting 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase, an enzyme catalyzing the conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate, a rate-limiting step in cholesterol biosynthesis. This inhibition reduces plasma cholesterol and lipoprotein levels by decreasing cholesterol synthesis in the liver and increasing the number of hepatic Low Density Lipoprotein (LDL) receptors on the cell surface for enhanced uptake and catabolism of LDL. Atorvastatin calcium lowers LDL-Cholesterol (LDL-C), Very Low Density Lipoprotein-Cholesterol (VLDL-C), serum triglycerides (TG), and Intermediate Density Lipoproteins (IDL), while increasing High Density Lipoprotein-Cholesterol (HDL-C). The reduction in LDL-C and apoB-containing particles is associated with a decreased risk of cardiovascular events and mortality. Atorvastatin calcium has been shown to be effective in reducing levels of total cholesterol, LDL-C, apoB, and total TG, and raising HDL-C levels in various patient populations, including those with familial hypercholesterolemia, mixed dyslipidemia, and hypertriglyceridemia. The lowering of total cholesterol, LDL-C, and apoB has been demonstrated to reduce the risk of cardiovascular events and mortality, while the increase in HDL-C is associated with decreased cardiovascular risk. The pharmacodynamic effects of atorvastatin calcium are most pronounced within 2-4 weeks of treatment, with a maximum effect observed within 4-6 weeks. The duration of action is sustained over time, with continued reduction in LDL-C and apoB levels. Special population considerations include the potential for increased risk of myopathy in patients with renal impairment, and the need for dose adjustment in patients with severe renal impairment.
Pregnancy Summary: Atorvastatin Calcium Tablets are contraindicated in pregnancy. The most dangerous trimester is the first trimester due to the risk of fetal malformations. Specific fetal/neonatal risks include hypotension and renal failure. If pregnancy occurs during treatment, the drug should be discontinued immediately and the patient should be referred to a specialist for further management.

Pharmacokinetics: Atorvastatin is rapidly absorbed after oral administration, with maximal plasma concentrations occurring within 1 to 2 hours, and its extent of absorption and plasma concentrations increase in proportion to the atorvastatin dose. The absolute bioavailability of atorvastatin is approximately 12%, and the systemic availability of HMG-CoA reductase inhibitory activity is approximately 30%, attributed to presystemic clearance in gastrointestinal mucosa and/or first-pass metabolism in the liver. Although food decreases the rate and extent of drug absorption by approximately 25% and 9%, as assessed by Cmax and AUC respectively, LDL-C reduction and HDL-C elevation are similar when atorvastatin is given with and without food. Plasma atorvastatin concentrations are lower (approximately 30% for Cmax and AUC) following drug administration in the evening compared with morning dosing, but LDL-C reduction and HDL-C elevation are the same regardless of the time of drug administration. Atorvastatin is extensively bound to plasma proteins, with a mean volume of distribution of approximately 381 liters and a blood/plasma ratio of approximately 0.25, indicating poor drug penetration into red blood cells. Atorvastatin is extensively metabolized to ortho- and para-hydroxylated derivatives by cytochrome P-450 3A4 (CYP 3A4) and to various beta-oxidation products, with approximately 70% of circulating inhibitory activity for HMG-CoA reductase attributed to active metabolites. Atorvastatin and its metabolites are eliminated by biliary excretion, with a mean plasma elimination half-life of approximately 14 hours, but the half-life for inhibitory activity for HMG-CoA reductase is 20 to 30 hours due to the contribution of longer-lived active metabolites. Less than 2% of a dose of atorvastatin is recovered in urine following oral administration. In special populations, plasma concentrations of atorvastatin are higher in healthy elderly subjects (approximately 40% for Cmax and 30% for AUC) compared with younger individuals, but LDL-C reduction is comparable to that seen in younger patient populations. Plasma concentrations of atorvastatin in women differ (approximately 20% higher for Cmax and 10% lower for AUC) from those in men, but there is no clinically significant difference in LDL-C reduction between men and women. Plasma concentrations of atorvastatin are similar in black and white subjects. In patients with chronic alcoholic liver disease (Childs-Pugh B), plasma concentrations of atorvastatin are markedly increased (approximately 16-fold in Cmax and 11-fold in AUC). In patients with moderate renal insufficiency, plasma concentrations and LDL-C lowering efficacy of atorvastatin calcium are similar compared with patients with normal renal function

Pharmacodynamics: Atorvastatin calcium is a synthetic lipid-lowering agent that selectively and competitively inhibits 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase, an early and rate-limiting step in the biosynthesis of cholesterol. This inhibition reduces the conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate, thereby lowering plasma cholesterol and lipoprotein levels. Atorvastatin calcium also increases the number of hepatic Low Density Lipoprotein (LDL) receptors on the cell surface, enhancing the uptake and catabolism of LDL. As a result, it reduces LDL-Cholesterol (LDL-C) and the number of LDL particles, as well as Very Low Density Lipoprotein-Cholesterol (VLDL-C), serum triglycerides (TG), and Intermediate Density Lipoproteins (IDL). Additionally, it increases High Density Lipoprotein-Cholesterol (HDL-C) levels. The lowering of total cholesterol, LDL-C, and ApoB has been shown to reduce the risk of cardiovascular events and mortality. Atorvastatin calcium has been demonstrated to be effective in reducing levels of total cholesterol, LDL-C, apoB, and total TG, and raising HDL-C levels in various patient populations, including those with familial hypercholesterolemia, mixed dyslipidemia, hypertriglyceridemia, and dysbetalipoproteinemia. The onset of action for atorvastatin calcium is not explicitly stated, but its effects are generally seen within a few weeks of treatment. The duration of action is also not specified, but it is likely to be several weeks, given its half-life of approximately 14 hours. Special population considerations include the potential for increased risk of myopathy in patients with renal impairment, and the need for dose adjustment in patients with severe renal impairment.
Pregnancy Summary: Atorvastatin calcium is contraindicated in pregnancy. The most dangerous trimester is the first trimester, where fetal risks include malformations. There is limited information available on the use of atorvastatin in pregnant women, and its use during pregnancy is not recommended. If pregnancy occurs during treatment, the medication should be discontinued immediately and the patient should be referred to a specialist for further management.

Pharmacokinetics: Atorvastatin is rapidly absorbed after oral administration, with maximal plasma concentrations occurring within 1 to 2 hours, and its extent of absorption and plasma concentrations increase in proportion to the atorvastatin dose. The absolute bioavailability of atorvastatin is approximately 12%, but the systemic availability of its HMG-CoA reductase inhibitory activity is approximately 30%, attributed to presystemic clearance in gastrointestinal mucosa and/or first-pass metabolism in the liver. Food decreases the rate and extent of drug absorption by approximately 25% and 9%, respectively, but LDL-C reduction and HDL-C elevation are similar when atorvastatin is given with and without food. Atorvastatin is extensively metabolized to ortho- and para-hydroxylated derivatives by cytochrome P-450 3A4 (CYP 3A4) and to various beta-oxidation products, with approximately 70% of circulating inhibitory activity for HMG-CoA reductase attributed to active metabolites. Atorvastatin is primarily eliminated in bile following hepatic and/or extrahepatic metabolism, with a mean plasma elimination half-life of approximately 14 hours, but the half-life for inhibitory activity for HMG-CoA reductase is 20 to 30 hours due to the contribution of longer-lived active metabolites. Plasma concentrations of atorvastatin are higher in healthy elderly subjects (approximately 40% for Cmax and 30% for AUC) compared with younger individuals, but LDL-C reduction is comparable to that seen in younger patient populations. Additionally, plasma concentrations of atorvastatin are similar in black and white subjects, but markedly increased in patients with chronic alcoholic liver disease (approximately 16-fold in Cmax and 11-fold in AUC). In patients with moderate renal insufficiency, plasma concentrations and LDL-C lowering efficacy of atorvastatin calcium are similar to those in patients with normal renal function, but the lowest dose should be used with caution.
